\chapter{The Simple Past}
\label{ch:ge-praeteritum}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can recognise the one-word past German uses in writing, produce the handful of its forms that people actually say out loud, and explain why the rest of it retreated.}

German's second past means exactly what the first one means, so this chapter separates the two by register rather than by tense: produce the Perfekt, recognise the Präteritum, and learn the short list of forms that ignore the rule. It ends with the reason the tense retreated at all — the same change ran through French and Italian over the same centuries, because their speakers are neighbours.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-te]{-te — the one-word past}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-praeteritum}



\begin{quote}
German has a second past tense. It needs no helper verb and no participle — just a stem and an ending.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: add -te to the stem}]
\begin{quote}
Take a regular verb's stem and put \textbf{-te} on it.
\end{quote}

The tense that ending builds is called the \emph{\textbf{Präteritum}}. Where the \emph{Perfekt} spends two words and a bracket, this one spends a single word: \emph{sag-} plus \emph{-te} and the sentence is done.

The two tenses report the same events. That is worth saying plainly, because a learner reasonably expects a language with two pasts to be drawing a distinction with them, the way English draws one between \emph{I said} and \emph{I have said}. German draws none. What separates its two pasts is something else entirely, and it takes a few more lessons to arrive at.

The \emph{-te} itself has a history reaching well beyond German, and that comes first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the recipe — \textquotedblleft{}stem plus te\textquotedblright{}
  \item the name — \textquotedblleft{}das Präteritum\textquotedblright{}
  \item how many words it takes — \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}stem plus -te.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending builds the \emph{Präteritum} on a regular verb? (\textbf{-te}.) How many words does it need? (\textbf{One}.) How many does the \emph{Perfekt} need? (\textbf{Two}.) Do the two tenses mean different things? (\textbf{No}.) Next: the first verb through the new ending.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich sagte]{ich sagte — \textquotedblleft{}I said,\textquotedblright{} in one word}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-sagte}



\begin{quote}
Run the new ending on the verb this chapter started from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich sagte}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich sagte} — \textquotedblleft{}I said.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Stem \emph{sag-}, ending \emph{-te}. Two syllables and it is finished, where the \emph{Perfekt} took three words to say the same thing:

\begin{quote}
\emph{ich \textbf{sagte}} · \emph{ich habe \textbf{gesagt}}
\end{quote}

Both are \textquotedblleft{}I said.\textquotedblright{} Neither is more past than the other, neither is more polite, and neither is wrong. Hold that in mind while the differences that do exist arrive.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{long-a} — the stem vowel is the same long \emph{a} as in \emph{sagen}; the new ending does not shorten it.
  \item \texttt{final-te} — the \emph{-te} is a full unstressed syllable, \emph{tuh}, not a bare \emph{t}. Hear the difference against the participle: \emph{ge-SAHKT} has one syllable at the end, \emph{SAHK-tuh} has two.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich sagte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair back to back — \textquotedblleft{}ich sagte … ich habe gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two endings apart — \textquotedblleft{}gesagt, sagte\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich sagte, ich habe gesagt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I said\textquotedblright{} in one word. (\textbf{Ich sagte}.) And in three. (\textbf{Ich habe gesagt}.) Which of them is further in the past? (\textbf{Neither}.) How many syllables does \emph{sagte} have? (\textbf{Two}.) Next: the same ending on the verb for doing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich machte]{ich machte — \textquotedblleft{}I made,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I did\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-machte}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{gemacht}. Build the other past of the same verb before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich machte}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich machte} — \textquotedblleft{}I made,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I did.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Mach-} plus \emph{-te}. Notice what the two pasts of this verb have in common: the stem. \emph{Gemacht} wrapped it and \emph{machte} suffixed it, and neither touched a letter inside it.

That is the whole promise of a weak verb. Whatever German asks of it, the middle stays put — which is why the four participles of the last chapter and the \emph{-te} forms of this one can be built from any regular verb you meet, on the spot, without a list.

\begin{quote}
\emph{er machte das} · \emph{er hat das gemacht}
\end{quote}

Same person, same event, two tenses.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich machte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}er machte das … er hat das gemacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item both new forms — \textquotedblleft{}sagte, machte\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich sagte, ich machte.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I did\textquotedblright{} in one word. (\textbf{Ich machte}.) What do \emph{machte} and \emph{gemacht} share? (\textbf{The stem} \emph{mach-}.) Does either change the stem? (\textbf{No}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}he did that\textquotedblright{} both ways. (\textbf{Er machte das}; \textbf{er hat das gemacht}.) Next: where that \emph{-te} came from, and the English ending that is the same thing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das dentale Präteritum]{The dental preterite — a Germanic invention}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-dentales-praeteritum}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{sagte}, then say \emph{walked}. Both endings are made with the tongue against the teeth, and that is not a coincidence.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The German \emph{-te} is what linguists call the \textbf{dental preterite}: a past tense made by bolting a \emph{t} or \emph{d} sound onto a stem. Dental, because those sounds are made at the teeth.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{past} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{sag-} & sag\textbf{te} \\
English & \emph{walk} & walk\textbf{ed} \\
Dutch & \emph{werk-} & werk\textbf{te} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three languages, one device, inherited rather than borrowed — this is a \textbf{Germanic invention}, and it is one of the features that identifies the family. Everything with a \emph{-t} or \emph{-d} past in Germanic comes from the same ancestor.

Latin built nothing of the kind. Its past came from inherited perfect endings and from reduplication, and its descendants carried that on: French \emph{parla}, Spanish \emph{habló}. So \emph{sagte} and \emph{walked} are one machine, and \emph{parla} and \emph{habló} are a different one — which is why an English speaker recognises the German ending on sight and a Spanish speaker does not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three together — \textquotedblleft{}sagte, walked, werkte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the name — \textquotedblleft{}the dental preterite\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two machines — \textquotedblleft{}sagte and walked; parla and habló\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sagte, walked — the same ending.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{-te} called? (\textbf{The dental preterite}.) Why \emph{dental}? (\textbf{It is made at the teeth}.) Which English ending is the same thing? (\textbf{-ed}.) Did Latin have it? (\textbf{No} — Romance builds its past another way.) Next: the one verb whose \emph{-te} form you will hear constantly.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich hatte]{ich hatte — \textquotedblleft{}I had\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-hatte}



\begin{quote}
The dental ending on the verb you have been leaning on for two chapters.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich hatte}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich hatte} — \textquotedblleft{}I had.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Haben} drops its \emph{b} — the same \emph{b} that goes missing in \emph{du hast} and \emph{er hat} — and the dental ending lands on what is left, doubling the \emph{t} in the spelling: \emph{hat-te}. Two syllables, both short.

English did the identical thing to the identical verb and then wore the result down further: \emph{have} lost its consonant and took a \emph{-d}, giving \emph{had}. So \emph{hatte} and \emph{had} are the same word doing the same job.

\emph{Haben} has a \emph{Perfekt} of its own as well — \emph{ich habe gehabt}, \textquotedblleft{}I have had\textquotedblright{} — built by the ordinary recipe, since \emph{haben} is a perfectly ordinary verb when it is not busy helping another one.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — the doubled \emph{tt} is one sharp \emph{t}, and the vowel in front of it is short and clipped. \emph{HAT-tuh}, never \emph{HAH-tuh}.
  \item \texttt{final-te} — the ending is still a full unstressed syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich hatte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}ich hatte … ich habe gehabt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English twin — \textquotedblleft{}hatte, had\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich hatte, ich hatte.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I had.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich hatte}.) Which letter of \emph{haben} is missing? (\textbf{The b}.) Say the same thing in the \emph{Perfekt}. (\textbf{Ich habe gehabt}.) Which English word is \emph{hatte}? (\emph{\textbf{Had}}.) Next: which of the two pasts a German actually reaches for, and where.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gesprochen oder geschrieben]{Which past, and where}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-register}



\begin{quote}
Two tenses, one meaning. Time to answer the question that has been waiting since the \emph{-te} arrived: when does a German say which?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: speech takes one, writing takes the other}]
\begin{quote}
The \emph{Perfekt} belongs to \textbf{speech}. The \emph{Präteritum} belongs to \textbf{narrative writing}.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{tense} & \textbf{where it lives} \\
\midrule
\emph{Perfekt} & everyday conversation, and dominant there \\
\emph{Präteritum} & novels, reports, anything told on the page \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Open a German novel and the story runs in \emph{Präteritum} from the first page to the last. Stand in a German kitchen and you will barely hear it. Neither audience thinks it is choosing a tense; each is simply doing what that setting does.

So the practical instruction for a speaker is lopsided and easy: \textbf{produce} the \emph{Perfekt}, \textbf{recognise} the \emph{Präteritum}. You will read far more of it than you will ever need to say.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
There is a second axis, and it is geographic. Spoken \emph{Präteritum} has largely vanished from conversation in southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland; further north it survives noticeably better. A Hamburg speaker will use forms in conversation that a Munich speaker would find bookish.

That map is not decoration — the next lessons turn out to explain it — and it means the honest answer to \textquotedblleft{}do Germans say \emph{ich sagte}?\textquotedblright{} is: some of them, some of the time, and it depends where you are standing.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the split — \textquotedblleft{}Perfekt for speech, Präteritum for writing\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own instruction — \textquotedblleft{}produce the Perfekt, recognise the Präteritum\textquotedblright{}
  \item the map — \textquotedblleft{}weaker in the south, stronger in the north\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Perfekt spoken, Präteritum written.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which past does a novel use? (\textbf{The Präteritum}.) Which does a conversation use? (\textbf{The Perfekt}.) Which should you produce? (\textbf{The Perfekt}.) Where is spoken \emph{Präteritum} weakest? (\textbf{The south}.) Next: the forms that ignore all of this and stay spoken everywhere.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich konnte]{ich konnte — \textquotedblleft{}I could\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-konnte}



\begin{quote}
The last new form of the chapter, and a \emph{Präteritum} nobody thinks twice about saying out loud.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich konnte}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich konnte} — \textquotedblleft{}I could,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I was able to.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The dental ending again, doubled in the spelling as it was in \emph{hatte}: \emph{konn-te}. It belongs to a small family of verbs German calls \emph{modal} — the ones that lean on another verb, the way English \emph{can}, \emph{must} and \emph{may} do.

Those verbs are the \emph{Präteritum}'s stronghold in ordinary speech. Nobody in Munich says \emph{ich habe gekonnt} over dinner; they say \emph{ich konnte}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Konnte} and English \emph{could} descend from one Germanic verb, *\emph{kunnaną}, which meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to know how}\textquotedblright{} rather than \textquotedblleft{}to be physically able.\textquotedblright{} Ability arrived later, out of knowledge.

That older sense is still visible in the English relatives: \emph{know}, \emph{cunning} (originally \textquotedblleft{}knowing\textquotedblright{}), and \emph{uncouth}, which began as \textquotedblleft{}unknown.\textquotedblright{} The \emph{l} that English wrote into \emph{could} is pure accident — it was copied from \emph{would} and \emph{should} centuries after anyone stopped pronouncing it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich konnte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two doubled forms — \textquotedblleft{}hatte, konnte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the old meaning — \textquotedblleft{}konnte, could — knew how\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich konnte, ich hatte.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I could.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich konnte}.) What did the verb behind it originally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To know how}.\textquotedblright{}) Name an English cousin. (\emph{\textbf{Know}}, \emph{cunning}, or \emph{uncouth}.) Is \emph{konnte} bookish? (\textbf{No} — it is said out loud everywhere.) Next: why a handful of forms get that exemption.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hatte, konnte]{The forms that stayed spoken}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-hochfrequent}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Hatte}. \emph{Konnte}. Both are \emph{Präteritum}, and both come out of a German mouth without a second thought. So the writing-only rule has holes in it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a short list of survivors}]
\begin{quote}
A handful of very common verbs keep their one-word past \textbf{in speech}, everywhere in the German-speaking world.
\end{quote}

Three groups make up almost the whole list:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hatte} — the past of \emph{haben};
  \item \textbf{konnte} and its modal siblings — \emph{musste}, \emph{wollte}, \emph{durfte};
  \item the past of the verb for \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} which arrives two chapters from now and is the most-said of them all.
\end{itemize}

Everything else in the \emph{Präteritum} obeys the split you learned last: written, not spoken.

Why these? Because they are the verbs said most often, and frequency protects a form the way it protects an irregularity. A shape you produce fifty times a day is never up for replacement; a shape you produce once a month quietly gets swapped for the compound version and nobody notices the swap happening.

So the practical list is genuinely short, and it is worth having by heart rather than by rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the survivors you own — \textquotedblleft{}hatte, konnte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the modal siblings — \textquotedblleft{}musste, wollte, durfte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reason — \textquotedblleft{}frequency protects a form\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}hatte, konnte — spoken everywhere.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name two \emph{Präteritum} forms a German says out loud. (\emph{\textbf{Hatte}}, \emph{\textbf{konnte}}.) Which family does \emph{konnte} belong to? (\textbf{The modals}.) Why did these survive? (\textbf{They are said most often}.) Next: why the rest of the tense retreated, and where the retreat came from.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[areale Veränderung]{The same retreat, three times over}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-praeteritum-map}



\begin{quote}
German is not the only language that let a two-word past crowd out a one-word one. Two of its neighbours did the identical thing at the identical time.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{one-word past} & \textbf{what took it over in speech} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{Präteritum} & \emph{Perfekt} \\
French & \emph{passé simple} & \emph{passé composé} \\
Italian & \emph{passato remoto} & \emph{passato prossimo} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two Romance languages and one Germanic one, doing the same thing over the same centuries — and not by coincidence. The dental \emph{-te} and the Romance endings came from completely different ancestors, so nothing inherited can account for three languages arriving at the same answer.

Geography can. Southern Germany, France and northern Italy are one connected block of territory, and the change spread through it by \textbf{contact}: speakers who live near each other borrow habits, and a habit of speech travels across a language boundary as easily as across a dialect one. Linguists call a change that spreads that way an \emph{\textbf{areal}} change.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Two pieces of evidence make the contact story stick rather than merely sound good.

The first is what did \textbf{not} happen at the western edge. Spanish and Portuguese kept their one-word past far more fully in speech, and they are the two languages furthest from that connected block.

The second is the map inside German itself, which you already met: the \emph{Präteritum} is weakest in the \textbf{south}, nearest the centre of the change, and strongest in the \textbf{north}, furthest from it. A change spreading outward from a region should thin as it goes, and that is exactly what German shows.

Geography did not dictate any single sentence. But it explains why a Germanic language and two Romance ones moved in step, and why one end of Germany sounds older than the other.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three languages — \textquotedblleft{}German, French, Italian: the same retreat\textquotedblright{}
  \item the name — \textquotedblleft{}an areal change, spread by contact\textquotedblright{}
  \item the inside map — \textquotedblleft{}south more Perfekt, north more Präteritum\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}areal change — it spread by contact.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two neighbours made the same change? (\textbf{French} and \textbf{Italian}.) Did German inherit it from Latin? (\textbf{No} — the two families build their pasts from different material.) What is a change that spreads by contact called? (An \emph{\textbf{areal}} change.) Which two languages at the western edge kept their one-word past? (\textbf{Spanish} and \textbf{Portuguese}.) Next: the chapter run through end to end.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the two pasts, side by side}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-praeteritum-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The point of this one is to hear, in your own voice, that two different-sounding sentences report the same event.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one meaning, two shapes}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{Präteritum} & \textbf{Perfekt} \\
\midrule
I said & \emph{ich sagte} & \emph{ich habe gesagt} \\
I made & \emph{ich machte} & \emph{ich habe gemacht} \\
I had & \emph{ich hatte} & \emph{ich habe gehabt} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say each pair back to back — \emph{ich sagte} … \emph{ich habe gesagt} — and then \emph{er machte das} … \emph{er hat das gemacht}. Nothing about the meaning has moved. All that has changed is which room you are standing in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}ich sagte … ich habe gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other pair — \textquotedblleft{}er machte das … er hat das gemacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item the survivors — \textquotedblleft{}ich hatte, ich konnte\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own instruction — \textquotedblleft{}produce the Perfekt, recognise the Präteritum\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich sagte, ich habe gesagt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I made\textquotedblright{} both ways. (\textbf{Ich machte}; \textbf{ich habe gemacht}.) Which of the two would a novel use? (\textbf{The Präteritum}.) Which would you say out loud? (\textbf{The Perfekt} — except for the survivors.) What is the \emph{-te} called? (\textbf{The dental preterite}.) What kind of change pushed the tense out of speech? (An \emph{\textbf{areal}} one.) Next: the verb every one of these sentences has been waiting for.
\end{tcolorbox}
